I THE PROLOGUE ROME

THE WORKERS

The grandeur of the Roman Empire was not built by emperors, but by the hands of its laborers. Discover the trades that shaped the ancient world.

753 BC — AD 476 · AN ARCHIVE OF ANCIENT LABOR

01 / CERAMICS

THEPOTTER

The wheel remembers the hand.

FIG. 01 THE VESSEL

Roman pottery, from fine red Samian ware to everyday amphorae, was essential for transporting olive oil, wine, and grain across the Mediterranean. Potters used fast-spinning wheels and massive kilns, turning humble clay into the vessels of global trade.

MATERIAL
CLAY · WHEEL · KILN
FORMS
AMPHORA · SAMIAN WARE
EXPORT
OIL · WINE · GRAIN

02 / GEOMATICS

THESURVEYOR

A line drawn before the city.

FIG. 02 THE LINE

Equipped with the Groma—a simple cross-shaped instrument used to measure straight lines and right angles—Roman surveyors (Gromatici) laid out the grid systems for military camps, roads, and new cities. Their precision engineering paved the way for the empire's infrastructure.

INSTRUMENT
GROMA · LIBELLA
SURVEYED
CAMPS · ROADS · CITIES
PRINCIPLE
THE RIGHT ANGLE

03 / ADMINISTRATION

THESCRIBE

What is written outlives the hand.

FIG. 03 THE RECORD

Behind every legion and tax record was a scribe. Working with reed pens (calami), ink, and papyrus or wooden wax tablets, these clerks recorded laws, kept census data, and managed supply chains. They were the silent engine of Roman bureaucracy.

TOOLS
CALAMUS · INK · WAX
RECORDED
LAWS · CENSUS · SUPPLY
SERVED
LEGION · TREASURY · STATE
